title: Fast On-Chip Thermometry with TiN Kinetic Inductance Resonators in 22 nm Process Technology
authors: Johann Drayne, George Ridgard, Lorenzo Peri, Frederic Schlattner, Fabio Olivieri, Mathieu de Kruijf, Isaac Harris, Grayson Noah, James Kirkman, Alberto Gomez-Saiz, M. Fernando Gonzalez-Zalba, Thomas Swift
abstract: Understanding the temporal and spatial dependence of temperature is critical in high-performance cryogenic devices. Typical thermometry techniques struggle to simultaneously combine high bandwidth, sensitivity and on-chip integration, limiting their ability to measure fast intra-device thermal fluctuations. Here, we demonstrate a time-resolved thermometry platform based on TiN kinetic inductance resonators integrated in a 22 nm FDSOI chip. By tracking temperature-dependent shifts in the resonant frequency, we achieve sub-millikelvin temperature sensitivity down to temperatures of 100 mK. Time-resolved on-chip pulsed heating experiments as a function of distance reveal an onset delay, consistent with a quasi-ballistic heat propagation velocity of 3.9 ${\pm}$ 0.1 mm $μ$s${}^{-1}$. We also show that elevated temperatures increase net thermal conductance, shortening thermal relaxation times across all spatial separations. This behaviour manifests in two distinct regimes: a substrate-limited regime at 100 mK, where cooling rates vary with heater distance, and a Kapitza boundary-limited regime at 400 mK, where thermal relaxation becomes more spatially uniform.These measurements demonstrate kinetic inductance thermometry's ability to rapidly probe non-equilibrium temperature dynamics in cryogenic devices such as quantum processors.
summary: This paper presents a novel, highly sensitive, on-chip thermometry platform using superconducting TiN resonators to measure temperature fluctuations in cryogenic environments. By performing time-resolved pulsed heating experiments, the authors quantified the speed and mechanism of heat dissipation, revealing that thermal transport is limited by substrate or interface resistance rather than the superconducting material itself. This capability is vital for designing and operating next-generation quantum processors.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately measuring fast, time- and distance-dependent temperature fluctuations within high-performance cryogenic devices like quantum processors.
main_result: The authors demonstrated sub-millikelvin temperature sensitivity and quantified the heat propagation velocity as $3.9 \pm 0.1 	ext{ mm } \mu	ext{s}^{-1}$, identifying the rate-limiting thermal bottlenecks at different cryogenic temperatures.
method: They employed a time-resolved thermometry platform using TiN kinetic inductance resonators integrated into a 22 nm FDSOI chip, measuring temperature via shifts in the microwave resonant frequency.
model_or_system: The system involves superconducting TiN films whose kinetic inductance ($L_k$) is temperature-dependent due to Cooper-pair depairing. Thermal dynamics are modeled using lumped-element approximations involving temperature-dependent heat capacity ($C_{total}$) and thermal conductance ($G_{total}$).
key_observables: Temperature-dependent resonant frequency shifts ($\partial f_r/\partial T$), thermal relaxation time ($	au_{	ext{cooling}}$), and the onset delay time ($t_0$).
important_parameters: Sub-millikelvin temperature sensitivity, heat propagation velocity ($3.9 	ext{ mm } \mu	ext{s}^{-1}$), and distinct thermal regimes (substrate-limited vs. Kapitza boundary-limited).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes kinetic inductance dominates over geometric inductance, and that the measured thermal response is limited by substrate or interface resistance rather than intrinsic superconducting recovery.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature dependence of the resonant response, the calculated temperature sensitivity ($\delta T$), and time-resolved measurements showing how thermal relaxation times ($	au_{	ext{cooling}}$) change with distance and temperature, revealing distinct physical regimes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the thermometry technique using kinetic inductance resonators. It then moves to time-resolved pulsed heating experiments to map thermal decay kinetics. Finally, it analyzes the distance dependence of the thermal relaxation time to determine the rate-limiting heat transport mechanism.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial, highly integrated, and quantitative tool for characterizing the thermal environment of quantum devices, which is essential for understanding decoherence mechanisms in solid-state quantum computing architectures.
